q: On a two-way radio failure, what transponder code do you select?
a: Change the transponder to code 7600.

src.ref: FOM 11.1.4 — Lost Communications – Two-Way Radio Failure
src.quote: If two-way radio failure occurs, change transponder code to 7600.
src.note: If the failure is in or later meets VFR conditions, continue VFR and land as soon as practicable; if in IFR, fly the Route/Altitude/Leave-Clearance-Limit rules of 14 CFR 91.185.

q: If you lose two-way radio and must enter the US ADIZ, what do you do and what code do you squawk?
a: Use emergency authority and enter the ADIZ as close to the Flight Plan crossing position and time as possible, squawking 7700; then follow standard comm-failure procedures.

src.ref: FOM 11.1.4.1 — Entering ADIZ without Radio Contact
src.quote: use emergency authority and enter the ADIZ as close to the Flight Plan crossing position and time as possible with transponder code 7700
src.note: Note the distinction: 7600 for the comm failure itself, but 7700 specifically to enter the ADIZ under emergency authority.

q: What temperature threshold makes an ill traveler a reportable communicable-disease case?
a: A temperature of 100 degrees F (38 degrees C) or greater that has persisted more than 48 hours (or fever with certain other symptoms, or diarrhea).

src.quote: has a temperature of 100°F (38°C) or greater which has persisted more than 48 hours
src.note: Contact MedLink and ensure Dispatch is notified; if the CDC quarantines the aircraft they may direct you to one of the 20 stations on the listed map.

q: Post-decompression, if oxygen needs exceed available masks or quantity, what descent target relieves adverse physiological reactions?
a: After terrain and fuel considerations, a descent to 8000 ft cabin altitude should eliminate adverse physiological reactions.

src.quote: a descent to 8000 ft cabin altitude, after terrain and fuel considerations are addressed, should eliminate any adverse physiological reactions
src.note: Enroute use or depletion of a POB imposes no restriction on flight operations and requires no pilot action.

q: What is the MedLink Inflight Medical Assistance phone number?

src.quote: MedLink Inflight Medical Assistance may be reached at (602) 282-4910
src.note: On the 787, when the Flight Crew calls MedLink they conference in the F/As with the cabin headset.

q: After extinguishing a lithium battery fire, why must you cool the device and how long can it take?
a: HALON extinguishes the fire but the device must then be cooled, preferably with water; it may take 15 or more minutes to fully cool. Avoid ice, which insulates and can let remaining cells reignite.

src.quote: It may take 15 or more minutes to completely cool the device.
src.note: AVOID USING ICE to cool the device; ice acts as an insulator, and an insulated but not-yet-cooled device can reignite.

q: Can water be used on a lithium battery fire?
a: Water may be used to fight a lithium ion battery fire, but should not be used on a lithium metal battery fire. Cool with water preferably, or any non-alcoholic liquid if water is not available.

src.quote: Water may be used to fight a lithium ion battery fire, but should not be used on a lithium metal battery fire.
src.note: FIGHT THE FIRE with a HALON extinguisher, then COOL THE DEVICE; non-alcoholic liquids such as milk, fruit juice, or POG are acceptable coolants.

q: What does emergency authority allow the Captain to do in a situation requiring immediate decision and action?
a: Take any action considered necessary, including deviating from prescribed procedures, methods, weather minimums, and regulations to the extent required in the interest of safety.

src.quote: the Captain may take any action considered necessary, including deviating from prescribed procedures, methods, weather minimums, and regulations to the extent required in the interest of safety
src.note: Emergency authority is granted to both the Captain and the Dispatcher; FOM 11.2.1 cites 14 CFR 91.3, 121.557, 121.559, 121.627, and Ops Spec A008.

q: Must you declare an emergency with ATC to use emergency authority?
a: No. The Captain may use emergency authority without declaring an emergency if traffic or handling priority is not needed, but should still advise ATC of intentions as soon as possible.

src.quote: The Captain may use emergency authority without declaring an emergency with ATC if traffic or handling priority is not needed.
src.note: The FOM adds: do not hesitate to declare an emergency if the situation warrants it.

q: Name situations the FOM says pilots will consider an emergency.
a: Fire or smoke endangering the aircraft; inability to definitely establish position; failure of a component jeopardizing safety of flight; an in-flight medical condition requiring a diversion; and a high probability of an emergency evacuation.

src.quote: An in-flight medical condition that requires a diversion
src.note: Immediately advise ATC and Dispatch; if workload is high or time short, ask ATC to notify the Company.

q: When should MAYDAY be used versus PAN-PAN?
a: MAYDAY (said three times) is the distress signal reserved for life-threatening situations; PAN-PAN (said three times) is the urgency signal for urgent situations that are not immediately life-threatening but require assistance.

src.ref: FOM 11.2.2.1 — Distress and Urgency Communication Signals
src.quote: Mayday should be reserved for life-threatening situations.
src.note: Pan-Pan is for urgent situations that are not immediately life-threatening but require assistance from someone on the ground.

q: What information belongs in an emergency message, and what is the Alaska HAZMAT emergency contact number?
a: Nature of emergency; number of passengers/crew and infants; passengers needing special assistance and their location; the HAZMAT emergency contact number if hazardous cargo is aboard (AS: 206-392-6465); and fuel remaining in minutes.

src.quote: If there is hazardous cargo on board, relay the HAZMAT emergency contact number:
src.note: The (AS) HAZMAT number is 206-392-6465; report fuel remaining in minutes.

q: After exercising emergency authority that deviates from FARs or company procedures, by when must a Captain file the safety report?
a: As soon as possible, but no later than the conclusion of the next mandatory 24-hour rest period. A Dispatcher who exercises emergency authority must report within 10 days.

src.quote: no later than the conclusion of the next mandatory 24-hour rest period
src.note: If the FAA later requests a written report and the crewmember fails to submit one, they may face punitive action including certificate action.

q: Is a minimum fuel advisory an emergency, and when should it be declared?
a: No, minimum fuel is not an emergency and does not imply a need for traffic priority; it should only be declared once the flight has committed to land at a specific airport, not while a divert option still exists.

src.quote: Minimum fuel is not an emergency situation, but merely indicates an emergency situation is possible should any undue delay occur.
src.note: Coordinate any divert decision with Dispatch before declaring; avoid ending up at an alternate with less than 30 minutes of fuel.

q: What must the PIC declare when landing will occur with less than a 30-minute fuel supply, and how is that 30 minutes defined?
a: Declare MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY, FUEL to ensure priority handling. The 30-minute supply is based on holding fuel flow or higher at 1500 ft above field elevation, and 30 minutes is a minimum the PIC may increase.

src.quote: the PIC shall declare, “MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY, FUEL” to ensure priority handling
src.note: The PIC must take every precaution to avoid landing with less than a 30-minute supply, based on holding fuel flow at 1500 ft above field elevation.

q: On a two-engine aircraft flying with one engine inoperative, what factors justify flying beyond the nearest suitable airport?
a: None. Sufficient fuel to fly farther, passenger accommodation other than safety, and availability of maintenance/repair are all specifically not sufficient justification to pass the nearest suitable airport.

src.quote: none of the following factors should be considered sufficient justification to fly beyond the nearest suitable airport
src.note: After an in-flight engine shutdown, land at the nearest suitable airport based on time considerations where a safe landing can be made (FOM 11.2.7).

q: How quickly are quick-don oxygen masks designed to be donned in an emergency descent?
a: With one hand within 5 seconds, because flight crews have very limited time of useful consciousness at altitude.

src.quote: Quick-don masks are designed to be donned with one hand within 5 seconds.
src.note: An emergency descent may be driven by loss of pressurization or other events such as fire or a cabin security incident.

q: For a 787 decompression over charted terrain polygons, how is the initial descent altitude determined?
a: On the 787, each region has an initial descent altitude specific to that region. If a decompression occurs within any polygon, the region-specific procedure should be executed to comply with passenger oxygen supply requirements.

src.quote: (787) Each region has an initial descent altitude specific to that region.
src.note: Escape procedures come in three types (Exit Any Direction, Exit Toward Fix, To Fix then Route); flights may not proceed through any “No Ops Area.”

q: What is the NTSB flight attendant briefing format, and what drives whether it is a normal or emergency landing?
a: N - Nature of the emergency, T - Time to prepare, S - Special instructions, B - Brace signal. The type of landing is based on the likelihood of evacuation, not on what is declared with ATC.

src.ref: FOM 11.2.11 — Abnormal/Emergency Briefing of Flight Attendants – NTSB
src.quote: The type of landing should be based on the likelihood of evacuation and not what is declared with ATC.
src.note: NORMAL LANDING means no evacuation prep required; EMERGENCY LANDING means evacuation is possible and the cabin should prepare.

q: When may the Cabin Crew initiate an evacuation on their own, and what memory aid lists the triggers?
a: If life-threatening conditions require immediate evacuation and they cannot communicate with the Captain after trying all reasonable means. The FAST acronym lists triggers: Flight Deck incapacitated, Aircraft impacted/at a peculiar angle, Smoke and fire present, Threat of imminent danger.

src.quote: Examples of Cabin Crew-initiated evacuation include (FAST acronym):
src.note: Flight Attendants are separately authorized to initiate an evacuation without Captain orders in an obvious life-threatening situation (FOM 11.2.12).

q: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: You've been holding for weather and it's now apparent you'll touch down with less than a 30-minute fuel supply. What exact call do you make, and how is that 30 minutes defined?
a: Declare "MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY, FUEL" to ensure priority handling. The 30-minute supply is based on holding fuel flow or higher, as required by configuration, at 1500 ft above field elevation; 30 minutes is a minimum the PIC may increase for runway-availability and go-around contingencies.

src.quote: When it becomes apparent that landing will occur with less than a 30-minute supply of fuel, the PIC shall declare, “MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY, FUEL” to ensure priority handling.
src.note: Do not confuse this with minimum fuel (11.2.5), which is not an emergency and grants no traffic priority.

q: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: Rapid decompression at cruise over charted high-terrain polygons in your 787. Walk me through the masks, the descent target that relieves physiological reactions, and how you pick the initial descent altitude.
a: Don quick-don masks (one hand, within 5 seconds), execute the region-specific escape procedure for the polygon you are in, and descend. On the 787 each region has its own initial descent altitude. After terrain and fuel are addressed, a descent to 8000 ft cabin altitude should eliminate adverse physiological reactions.

src.quote: If a decompression occurs within any polygon, the region-specific procedure should be executed in order to comply with passenger oxygen supply requirements.
src.note: (787) Each region has an initial descent altitude specific to that region. Quick-don masks are designed to be donned with one hand within 5 seconds (11.2.8).

q: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: A passenger collapses two hours into an overwater leg. Who do you contact, who has final authority on whether to divert, and how does the 787 loop the flight attendants into the call?
a: Contact MedLink Inflight Medical Assistance at (602) 282-4910; with MedLink's advice and Dispatch, the Captain determines whether a medical diversion is necessary and coordinates diversion-airport preferences. Company policy is to follow MedLink's recommendation, but the Captain retains final authority on any operational request. On the 787 the Flight Crew conferences in the F/As with the cabin headset.

src.quote: the Captain will determine whether a medical diversion is necessary and coordinate with Dispatch and MedLink for diversion airport preferences.
src.note: MedLink Inflight Medical Assistance: (602) 282-4910. (787) The Flight Crew will conference in F/As with cabin headset (11.1.9.3).

q: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: You shut an engine down in flight. A field 20 minutes closer has a shorter runway; your maintenance base is 90 minutes ahead with plenty of fuel to reach it. Where do you land, and does the extra fuel or the maintenance base justify pressing on?
a: Land at the nearest suitable airport, based on time considerations, where a safe landing can be made. On a two-engine aircraft with one engine inoperative, neither sufficient fuel to fly farther, nor passenger accommodation other than safety, nor availability of maintenance/repair justifies flying beyond the nearest suitable airport.

src.quote: If an engine fails or is shut down in flight, land the aircraft at the nearest suitable airport, based on time considerations, where a safe landing can be made.
src.note: Per 11.2.7.1, none of these justify passing the nearest suitable airport: extra fuel, passenger accommodation other than safety, or maintenance/repair availability.
